title: Deliver Jaw-Dropping Moments
coreMove: Stage one peak moment that makes the idea unforgettable without stealing attention from it.
sourcePressure: The source centers surprise, demonstration, props, statistics, pictures, videos, headlines, personal stories, and high-note endings. Bill Gates, Jill Bolte Taylor, and Steve Jobs anchor surprise, physical props, and staged reveals that clarify the point.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version says create a stunt. The useful version says make one unforgettable peak serve the message so memory has something clean to keep.

sourceAnchors.name: Bill Gates malaria-mosquito demonstration
sourceAnchors.detail: the source identifies Gates releasing mosquitoes during a malaria talk as a brief surprise that clarified the scale and urgency of the problem
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The mosquito moment worked because the room felt the distance between comfort and malaria collapse for a second.

sourceAnchors.name: Jill Bolte Taylor's real human brain
sourceAnchors.detail: the source names Taylor's use of a real human brain as a physical prop that made the talk vivid and memorable
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Jill Bolte Taylor did not describe the brain as an abstraction when the object itself could stop the room.

sourceAnchors.name: Steve Jobs iPhone reveal
sourceAnchors.detail: the source names Jobs as an anchor for staged reveal and product demonstration, including merging three announced products into one device
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Steve Jobs turned the reveal into a memory hook by letting three familiar categories collapse into one object.

hook: audience gasps at a shocking statistic
speaker pulls a surprise prop from a bag
counterintuition: big moments are more important than content

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person 'You' direct address, retrospective 'It took her three weeks to see', question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

exampleSpecs.audience: a safety officer briefing office staff who ignore evacuation packets
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether staff remember how fast smoke changes a familiar hallway
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she turns off the conference-room lights, lets a smoke-simulation photo fill the wall, and has staff trace their exit with the image still visible
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a dark conference room lit by a gray hallway photograph

exampleSpecs.audience: a trainer teaching new screeners why small objects matter
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether trainees remember one overlooked shape after hours of image review
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he freezes one X-ray image, asks what is harmless, then overlays the hidden blade outline so the reveal trains attention rather than fear
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a blue X-ray screen glowing above a row of plastic trays

exampleSpecs.audience: a nurse educator explaining blood-sugar spikes to newly diagnosed adults
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the group remembers how quickly a normal lunch can change the number
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she places two glucose-meter photos beside the same lunch tray and reveals the ninety-minute difference only after everyone has guessed
exampleSpecs.firstImage: steam rising from a paper bowl beside a glucose meter photo

exampleSpecs.audience: an architect asking a council to save a train station facade
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the council remembers the building as civic memory, not a cost item
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he waits until the demolition cost slide, then lays a soot-blackened ticket-window brick on the table and lets it reset the room before speaking
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a soot-dark brick wrapped in brown paper on a council table

exampleSpecs.audience: a rescue director showing donors why a new intake room matters
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the donors remember capacity through one concrete bottleneck
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: you watch him stop outside the crowded intake shelf, lift one empty carrier, and let the silence reveal why three more cages matter
exampleSpecs.firstImage: an empty animal carrier scraping against a metal shelf

exampleSpecs.audience: a quality manager explaining a recall to warehouse supervisors
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the supervisors remember the one label flaw that can trigger a second recall
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: when someone says the labels look identical, he projects them at wall size and flips between them until the missing lot digit becomes impossible to miss
exampleSpecs.firstImage: two shipping labels flickering on a white warehouse wall

skillTargets: distinguish a meaningful peak from a stunt
choose a prop or reveal that clarifies the idea
evaluate when a wow moment hijacks the message

tryThisNowSpec: Choose the one point in your talk people must remember tomorrow, then design one object, reveal, contrast, or image that makes that point visible in under twenty seconds.

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
